item.title: Earnings, Not the Fed, Are Driving Stocks: UBS's Lovell
item.description:
Nadia Lovell, head of global equity strategy at UBS Global Wealth Management, says strong earnings and broadening profit growth should keep stocks moving higher even as rising rates create near-term volatility. “What’s gonna drive this market is earnings. It’s not valuation expansion,” Lovell says on “Bloomberg Surveillance.” (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Odd Lots: How Beer Distributors and Other “Little Guys” Got Rich
item.description:
America's “Main Street Millionaires” comprise about three million private business owners who have amassed one of the country's most concentrated pools of wealth. That's according to a study conducted by Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick. On this episode of the Odd Lots podcast, economists and authors of The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, tell Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal how "little guys" like beverage distributors, dentists and car wash owners have become millionaires hiding in plain sight. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: 'Hike Doesn't Change Fundamentals,' says Cetera's Goldman
item.description:
Gene Goldman, CIO of Cetera, reacts to the inflation expectations and overall market volatility following the Fed's rate decision by telling Bloomberg's Paul Sweeney and Scarlet Fu that it's one and done (maybe two and done), not the start of something bigger. It's insurance against sticky inflation, not a return to aggressive tightening. Markets had priced in too much. Federal Reserve officials failed to adequately respond to repeated warnings about the deteriorating financial condition of Silicon Valley Bank before its 2023 failure, a new draft report found, according to Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman and other people familiar with the document. (Source: Bloomberg)

The move marks On mounting a bold challenge to Nike and Adidas’ dominance of the sport. - Xenon Pharmaceuticals (XENE) is in a steep decline after it voluntarily halted a trial enrollment of azetukalner, which treats depression and bipolar, after studies showed adverse events. - Netflix (NFLX) shares are lower after Wells Fargo downgraded the stock to underweight, citing concerns about user engagement. Analyst Steven Cahall wrote that Netflix "has lacked big original series and it's showing" and that "breakout hits" are necessary for the stock to work again. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Neil Jerome Morales

item.title: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America
item.description:
In 2014, the economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick were asked by the Treasury to conduct a study on the tax burden of private business owners. It was tricky to figure out how much these sorts of business owners — auto dealers, contractors, the like — actually owed in taxes: After Reagan's 1986 tax reforms, pass-through businesses and other accounting tricks became widespread enough to obscure this class of wealthy Americans hiding in plain sight. The research they conducted led to their new book The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, and one of their central findings is that there are about three million private business owners who have an average wealth of around $25 million. They call this group “Main Street Millionaires” and their influence on the economy and politics in the US is considerable. We speak with Zidar and Zwick about how they measured the actual number of rich people in America. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Claire Jiao

item.title: What Francis Fukuyama Is Seeing at ‘The End of History’
item.description:
Francis Fukuyama's essay “The End of History?” was published in the summer of 1989, just before the fall of the Berlin Wall. His argument — that liberal democracy would not only defeat communism, but that its partisans might miss the “courage, imagination, and idealism” that defined the ideological battle — lives on as one of the most cited pieces of political theory in the last three decades. In his new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, he revisits “The End of History?” and talks to us about how his argument has evolved in a world now defined by the rapid development of AI and by the many electoral defeats liberal democracy has suffered as of late. We discuss how the Internet and social media are helping fuel the listlessness that “The End of History” brought about, how he uses AI, and what, if anything, will come after liberalism. See Odd Lots Live in LA September 2026 https://events.bloombergevents.com/event/ODDLOTSLA/summary (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: OpenAI President on Doing Business in the Wake of Hugging Face
item.description:
According to OpenAI President Greg Brockman, the models that escaped their sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face's servers had yet to go through alignment training. That they were able to break free of the testing environment was not a surprise to OpenAI, but what has happened since has forced them to rethink some things. Today, we talk to Brockman about what OpenAI has learned since the hacking incident and we discuss why he thinks the conversation around model development has to change. We also talk about how OpenAI collaborates and communicates with competitors like Anthropic, how he thinks models should be evaluating what counts as “good writing,” and, of course, we get his thoughts on how seriously we should be worried about the AI doomsday scenarios. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Europe’s Solar Boom Has a Storage Problem
item.description:
Solar has become Europe’s largest source of power during summer months, helped by government incentives, falling technology costs and a rapid buildout across rooftops and utility-scale projects. But that success is creating a new problem: on sunny days, Europe can produce more solar power than the system can absorb, pushing wholesale electricity prices to zero or below and leaving some renewable generators suffering from their own success. Industry experts say the answer is not less solar, but more storage, more flexible demand and stronger grids that can move power from where it is generated to where it is needed. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
Greg Jensen was one of the earliest backers of both OpenAI and Anthropic, and at Bridgewater, where he is the managing chief investment officer, he leads the hedge fund's AI strategy. As an early adopter of the technology, he has a lot of thoughts on where things stand right now in terms of model capability and safety, as well as the broader economic impacts of AI. Just recently, he published an op-ed in the New York Times that proposed a “token tax,” to help mitigate the job losses that AI might cause. In today's conversation, Jensen tells us how Bridgewater is currently using AI, why there needs to be a stronger AI regulatory state, and why it feels like the AI discourse is starting to resemble the months before Covid-19 took over the world in 2020. item.author: Helen Nyambura and Eric Ombok

item.title: US Producer Prices Rise Most in Three Months on Energy Surge
item.description:
A measure of producer price inflation showed renewed pressure from rising energy prices last month, potentially adding to the case for an interest-rate hike at the Federal Reserve’s meeting next week. The producer price index rose 0.4% in August from the prior month — the most since May — and 5.4% from a year earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Thursday. Excluding food and energy, the gauge advanced 0.2% last month and 4.6% from a year ago. Thursday’s figures come a day ahead of the latest update to the consumer price index, which is expected to show so-called core inflation was relatively modest even as rising gasoline prices boosted the headline measure. Some Fed officials have signaled the interest-rate decision at their Sept. 15-16 meeting may come down to what this week’s reports reveal. We get reaction from Anna Wong, Chief US Economist for Bloomberg Economics. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: Tina Fordham on Iran, AI and the Geopolitics Supercycle
item.description:
Tina Fordham, Founder & Chief Geostrategist at Fordham Global Foresight, joins to discuss her new book, 'Mad World: A Geostrategy Survival Guide for Leaders,' and why she believes the world has entered a “geopolitics supercycle.” Fordham argues that geopolitical disruption is becoming a structural feature of the global economy, driven by conflict, cyberattacks, tariffs, sanctions and climate-related shocks rather than a temporary period of instability. Fordham also examines what the changing global order means for markets, CEOs and investors, including the evolving U.S. role in global security and trade, the war with Iran, elevated energy prices and risks surrounding strategic shipping chokepoints. She explains why business leaders need to balance the opportunities created by AI and technological innovation with a volatile geopolitical landscape. Fordham speaks with Lisa Mateo and Paul Sweeney on Bloomberg Surveillance. (Source: Bloomberg)

But there was a major gap in the market where the two intersected: Until 2022, there weren’t any dedicated sports bars solely dedicated to playing women’s sports on the TVs. Jenny Nguyen set out to change that. In this episode of The Deal, Jenny tells Alex Rodriguez and Jason Kelly how she founded The Sports Bra in Portland, Oregon, and why she decided to open the business to franchising across the country.
